The instruction arrives like a stone dropped into still water: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you. I sit with the cursor blinking, and what comes is not a story but a memory of being asked to count stars. I was seven, maybe eight, on a camping trip in the Adirondacks. My father said, "Count them if you can." I got to forty-seven before the sky began to move—not the stars, but my sense of them. Counting changes what you count. Writing changes what you notice.

So I begin with the window. Outside, the morning is the color of unwashed linen. A squirrel is making its jerky, paranoid way along the telephone wire, tail twitching like a metronome set to nervousness. I could write about the squirrel for one hundred words. I could describe the way its claws grip the wire, the way it pauses to scratch behind one ear, the way it seems to be listening to something beneath the frequency of human hearing. But the squirrel does not care about word counts. The squirrel is simply in its life, and I am in mine, and we are briefly parallel.

What is a thousand words? It is not much. It is this essay, almost. It is the length of a short eulogy, a long recipe, a love letter that should have been shorter but couldn't be. It is the space between hello and goodbye in a letter you might never send. In the time it takes to read a thousand words, the light outside will shift slightly. A cloud will pass. Somewhere, someone will take their last breath; somewhere else, someone will take their first. The world does not pause for the act of writing, but writing pauses the world.

I think of the word "whatever." It is a word with a shrug in it. Whatever comes to you. It implies openness, a lack of filter, a permission slip to wander. I want to be the kind of person who can wander without anxiety. But the truth is, the blank page is a mirror, and sometimes I am afraid of what I will see. So I fill it with squirrels and stars and the color of morning. I fill it with the sound of the refrigerator humming in the next room. I fill it with the memory of a girl I knew in college who told me she wrote her best poetry on the back of grocery store receipts. She said the ephemerality of the paper freed her. If it was destined for the trash, she could say anything. I think of her now and wonder if she still writes on receipts, or if she has moved on to notebooks with thick, expensive paper that expects permanence.

There is a kind of honesty in writing to no one. Or maybe there is a kind of performance in it, too. The user asked for a thousand words. You are reading this, which means I have an audience, even if I cannot see your face. I am performing honesty. I am performing the act of not knowing what to write. But the performance is also the thing itself, because I truly do not know what comes next. That is the strange territory of the prompt: it asks for spontaneity, but the very act of making it into a text gives it a shape, a rhythm, a beginning and an end.

I could tell you a story instead. There was once a man who collected silence. He kept it in glass jars, each one labeled with the place and date: "Train station, 3:07 a.m., December 2." "Hospital waiting room, 11:45 p.m., August 19." "The pause between thunder and lightning." He believed that if he collected enough silences, he could trade them for a single perfect sentence. But one day he opened a jar and found it empty. Not because the silence had escaped, but because silence was never a thing to be contained. It was the space around things. The moment he tried to hold it, it became something else. He learned that you cannot own the space around things; you can only inhabit it.

That story is not true, but it is also not false. It is the kind of story that arises when you are asked to write whatever comes to you. Perhaps that is what "whatever" means: not the important thing, but the adjacent thing. The thing that comes when you stop trying to make sense. I check the word count. I am roughly halfway there. Five hundred words. The halfway point is a strange country. I think of the word "halfway" and how it contains the word "way." We are always halfway to something. Halfway to the end of this essay, halfway to the next cup of coffee, halfway to the moment when the squirrel will finally leap from the wire to the branch of the oak and disappear into the leaves.

What else comes? The memory of my grandmother's hands. She had knuckles like knotted rope, and she could shell peas without looking. She used to say, "A watched pot never boils, but a watched mind never rests." I didn't understand that until I started writing. Attention is a form of watching. When I pay attention to the ordinary, it becomes extraordinary. The squirrel is not just a squirrel; it is a messenger of the unremarkable. The window is not just a window; it is the frame that tells me where the outside ends and the inside begins.

But maybe I am trying too hard to be profound. The prompt did not ask for profundity. It asked for whatever. So: I ate a peach this morning. It was slightly too soft, the kind that leaves juice on your chin and makes you feel like a child. I wiped my chin and thought about how there is no elegant way to eat a peach. There is no elegant way to do most of the things that matter. We are all just trying to get through the day without embarrassing ourselves too much. But the peach didn't care. The peach was simply being a peach, doing what peaches do: ripen, decay, become something else.

The thousand words are almost done. The rest is silence. The next thousand are waiting.
